newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croatia's cenbank sets monetary policy targets.
newsitem.headline: Croatia's cenbank sets monetary policy targets.

text.p: Croatia's central bank governor said the growth of money aggregates will slow in 1997 while inflation will remain between three and four percent and the value of the domestic currency kuna will be stable.

Marko Skreb, governor of the National Bank of Croatia, said the broadest money aggregate M4, representing total liquid assets, is expected to continue growing this year but at a rate lower than in 1996, when it was around 40 percent.
"In 1997, just as last year, we continue with the post-stabilisation period, characterised by the process of remonetisation," Skreb told Reuters in an interview.

Croatia embarked on an austere stabilisation programme in October 1993, when monthly inflation ran at some 28 percent due to war and a deep recession caused by the fall of communism and the break-up of former Yugoslavia.
The crash programme immediately slashed inflation to zero, paving the way for the introduction of the kuna in 1994.
The M4 monetary aggregate has tripled since then and stands at around 37 billion kuna. The M1 money supply is put at 11.5 billion.
Skreb said the main tool for creating money would continue to be central bank interventions on foreign exchange markets.
"The purchase of foreign currency will be somewhat smaller than last year, but we expect to increase our net reserves by $450-500 million," Skreb said.
Croatia's total currency reserves topped $4 billion in January, with the central bank accounting for $2.1 and commercial banks $1.9 billion.
Skreb ruled out any easing of the exchange rate, rejecting demands by powerful export and tourist industry lobbies.
The kuna has appreciated slightly against the German mark in the last three years, firming to around 3.5 per mark from 3.7 when it was introduced in May 1994.

"If any, there is pressure for appreciating the kuna against the basket of foreign currencies," Skreb said, adding that the pressure will come from an expected inflow of foreign loans and direct investments.
Direct foreign investments are expected to grow this year some three to four times from a relatively modest $280 million last year, Skreb said.
Outlining the main features of monetary policy and central bank expectations for 1997, Skreb said inflation would remain in the three-to-four-percent range, as in the past two years.
December-on-December inflation was 3.4 percent in 1996 and 3.7 percent in 1995.
"Inflation will stay at current levels, between three and four percent annually, not more," Skreb said.
